CQ13.brief: In Sequencer, a character is animated with an Animation track. You place animation clips on the track as sections, and where two sections overlap Unreal blends from one clip to the next. You can also trim, loop, split, slow down and reverse each section. In this quest you put a mannequin into a sequence and practice all of these edits on two clips.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template. Drag a Skeletal Mesh, for example SKM_Manny, into the level.
Create a Level Sequence named LS_CharacterTest. With the mesh selected, click Add Track (+) and choose Actor to Sequencer. Check that an Animation track and a Transform track were created.
On the Animation track, click Add Animation (+) and pick an idle clip. Then add a walk or run clip, and place it so that the two sections overlap by about 20 frames.
Drag the blend handle on the overlap to make the blend longer. Right-click the blend curve and try a different curve shape from Options.
Drag the right edge of the second clip outward so that the clip loops. Put the playhead in the middle of it and press Ctrl + / to split the section into two parts.
Right-click one section and open Properties. Set Play Rate to 0.5, and enable Reverse on the part you split off. Then play the sequence.
CQ13.done_when: Send a screenshot of Sequencer that shows the Animation track with two overlapping clips and a visible blend, one looped section with notches, and the Properties menu open with Play Rate 0.5.

CQ14.brief: A shot that you can only see in the viewport cannot be shared with anyone. Movie Render Queue, often shortened to MRQ, is the tool that renders a Level Sequence to image files at final quality. In this quest you enable the tool, add your sequence as a render job, choose a few settings, save them as a preset, and render about 60 frames as PNG images.
checklist: Enable the Movie Render Pipeline plugin. Open Edit > Plugins, look under Built-In, and turn it on. Restart the editor if it asks you to.
Open Window > Cinematics > Movie Render Queue. Click + Render and add your Level Sequence, or drag it in from the Content Browser.
Click Unsaved Config* to open the settings of the job. Use + Setting to add .png Sequence [8bit], Deferred Rendering and Anti-aliasing.
In Anti-aliasing, set Spatial Sample Count to 1 and Temporal Sample Count to 8. Enable Override Anti Aliasing Mode and set it to None.
In Output, set an Output Directory, which is the folder where the images are saved. Keep the resolution 1920x1080. Enable Use Custom Playback Range and render only about 60 frames.
Open Presets and choose Save As Preset. Name the preset MRQ_Preview. Then click Render (Local) and wait until the preview window closes.
Open the output folder with the link in the Output column and check the PNG files.
CQ14.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Movie Render Queue window with your job and the MRQ_Preview preset selected. Also send a screenshot of the output folder that shows the PNG frame files.

CQ15.brief: This quest joins the skills from the earlier quests into one complete cinematic. You build a short sequence from shots, start it from gameplay, and render it to image files. It is the first time you go through the whole process from building to final frames.
checklist: Build LS_First, a master sequence that is 15 seconds long. It needs a Shots track with at least 2 shots, and each shot has its own Cine Camera.
Put a character with at least one Animation clip in one of the shots. Blend or trim the clip so that it fits the shot.
Add a Camera Cuts track so that the master sequence cuts between the two cameras at a clear moment in the action.
Start LS_First from the Level Blueprint with a Box Trigger. Use Set Playback Position with the value 0 and then Play. Add an F key event that skips the sequence with Go to End and Stop.
Add LS_First to Movie Render Queue. Use your MRQ_Preview preset and render the full 15 seconds as a PNG sequence.
Write 5 lines that say what each shot shows and name one problem you fixed.
CQ15.done_when: Send these to a mentor: a short video or GIF of the sequence playing in Play In Editor after you enter the trigger, a screenshot of the Level Blueprint, a screenshot of the Shots track, and a screenshot of the folder that lists the rendered PNG files, together with your 5-line note.

CQ16.brief: Take Recorder is a tool that records what happens while the game runs and saves it as a Level Sequence. Recording a character or a camera is often faster than setting keys by hand. Each recording is called a take, and every take is saved, so you keep all your attempts. In this quest you record your player character walking around, review the recording, and record a second take.
checklist: Enable the Take Recorder plugin in Edit > Plugins and restart the editor.
Open Window > Cinematics > Take Recorder. Set the Slate name to Walk and the take number to 1. The slate is the name that groups your takes.

Add your player character as a source, which is a thing that will be recorded. Click + Source and choose From Actor, or drag the character from the Outliner into Sources. Set Record Type to Spawnable.
Also add Camera Cuts as a source.
Press Play in the editor, then click the red Record button. Walk and turn for about 10 seconds. Then press the button again, or press Esc, to stop.
Click Review Last Recording. Then open the Takes Browser and find the take under Cinematics > Takes.
Record a second take with the same slate. Check that the take number went up to 2.
CQ16.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Take Recorder panel with your two sources. Also send a screenshot of the recorded sequence open in Sequencer that shows the recorded transform and animation tracks.

CQ17.brief: An Event Track lets a sequence run Blueprint logic at an exact frame, for example to play a sound, start an effect or open a door. The logic lives in the Director Blueprint, a Blueprint that belongs to the Level Sequence. Each event key calls an endpoint, which is a custom event inside that Blueprint. In this quest you make one event that passes a value to its endpoint, and a second event that calls a function on an actor in the sequence.
checklist: Open LS_Cutscene, or any other sequence. Click Add Track (+), then Event Track, then Trigger. Add a key at frame 60.
Right-click the key, open Properties, then Unbound, and choose Create New Endpoint. The Director Blueprint opens. Rename the endpoint to SpawnFX.
In the Director Blueprint, connect SpawnFX to a Spawn Emitter at Location node, or to a node that prints a string, so that something visible happens.

Select the endpoint and click Add Parameter (+). Name the parameter Scale and make it a float, which is a number with decimals. On the key, set the Payload value to 2.0, and use the value in the graph.
Add a second Event Track under an actor that is bound in the sequence, for example a light. Use Quick Bind to call Set Visibility on that actor.
Enable Call In Editor on the first key. Drag the playhead over frame 60 and see the event fire without pressing Play.
CQ17.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Director Blueprint that shows the SpawnFX endpoint with the Scale parameter and the Quick Bind event that is bound to the object. Also send a screenshot of the Sequencer timeline with both Event tracks.

CQ18.brief: The settings of a Movie Render Queue job decide if you get a noisy preview or a clean final frame. The most important ones are the file format, the number of samples (how many times each frame is rendered and averaged to smooth edges and motion blur), and where the files are saved. In this quest you build a final-quality settings list, save it as a preset, and render with it.
checklist: Open Window > Cinematics > Movie Render Queue and add your sequence as a job. Check that the Map field shows the correct level.
Open the Settings of the job. Delete the default .jpg Sequence [8bit] export. Add an EXR Sequence and a .png Sequence [8bit].
Add the Anti-Aliasing setting. Set Temporal Sample Count to 8 and Spatial Sample Count to 1. Enable Override Anti-Aliasing and set the method to None.
Add the Console Variables setting. Add one variable that raises quality, for example a higher value for r.MotionBlurQuality. Note that the variable goes back to its old value after the render.
In Output, set File Name Format to {sequence_name}/{shot_name}.{frame_number} and enable Auto Version. Set the Output Directory to a folder named Renders.
Save the settings as a preset named MRQ_Final. Then click Render (Local).
Extra: switch the job to Movie Render Graph and make a new graph asset. Find where Temporal Samples and Spatial Samples are set in the graph.
CQ18.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Render Settings window that shows your settings list (Output, Anti-Aliasing, Console Variables, and the EXR and PNG exports). Also send a screenshot of the output folder with both an .exr frame and a .png frame. Add one sentence that says why you turned TAA off.

CQ19.brief: In film, the light is set up again for every shot, because what looks good from one camera can look bad from another. Unreal gives you two tools for this. A Spawnable light exists only while its shot plays, and a lighting channel makes a light affect only the objects that use the same channel. In this quest you give two shots their own lights and lock the exposure so that the brightness does not change by itself.
checklist: Open a sequence that has at least 2 shots. In shot 1, drag a Spot Light from the Place Actors panel into Sequencer, so that it becomes a Spawnable. Name it L_Key_Shot01.
Set the Mobility of the light to Movable. Set the character or hero mesh (the main subject of the shot) to Movable too.
On L_Key_Shot01, open Light, then Advanced, and enable only Lighting Channel 1. On the hero mesh, enable Channel 1 in its Lighting category. Confirm that this light does not light the background.
Add keyframes on the Intensity track and the Light Color track, so that the key light changes during shot 1.

Add a Post Process Volume and enable Infinite Extent. Set Exposure Metering Mode to Manual and choose a fixed Exposure Compensation. Drag the playhead between the shots and confirm that the brightness does not drift.
Do the same for shot 2 with a second spawnable light. Play the sequence and check that each light exists only in its own shot.
CQ19.done_when: Send two screenshots, one of shot 1 and one of shot 2 in the viewport. Each must show the Sequencer outliner with its spawnable light (lightning bolt icon) and the Details panel with the Lighting Channel settings. Add one sentence that says why you used Manual exposure.

CQ20.brief: Color grading means changing the colors, contrast and brightness of the finished picture to give it a certain look. In Unreal you do this in a Post Process Volume, an actor that changes how the image looks inside its area. A base volume holds the look of the whole project, and smaller volumes with a higher Priority change single shots. In this quest you set up both, try a LUT (a small texture that remaps colors), and give a camera its own lens look.
checklist: Place a Post Process Volume and name it PPV_Grade_Base. Enable Infinite Extent (Unbound) and set Priority to 0. This volume holds the look of the whole project.
In PPV_Grade_Base, set the Film settings (Slope, Toe, Shoulder) once. Do not change them again after that.

Add a second volume named PPV_Shot02 around the area of shot 2. Give it Priority 1 and a Blend Radius. Grade it in Color Grading: first use Global (Saturation, Contrast, Gamma), then Shadows and Highlights.
Set Temperature Type to White Balance. Adjust Temp until white objects look white under your key light.

Take a high-resolution screenshot and build a LUT from it in an image editor. Import the LUT, set Mip Gen Settings to NoMipMaps and Texture Group to Color Lookup Table, and try it in Color Grading, under Global. Then turn the LUT off and match the same look with the grading wheels.
On your Cine Camera, set Post Process Blend Weight to 1 and add a small Vignette. This way the camera carries its own lens look.
Extra: create an OpenColorIO Configuration Asset and add a Color Output setting to your MRQ job.
CQ20.done_when: Send before and after screenshots of one shot (one without the grade and one with it). Also send a screenshot of the Details panel of PPV_Shot02 that shows Priority, Blend Radius and your Color Grading values. Add one sentence that says why the Film settings are only in the base volume.

CQ21.brief: An actor in a sequence is bound to it in one of two ways. A Possessable is an actor that already exists in the level, and the sequence only takes control of it. A Spawnable is created by the sequence when it plays and removed when it ends. Choosing the wrong type is a common reason why a cinematic breaks when the level changes. In this quest you create both types, convert one into the other, and change who owns a spawned actor.
checklist: Create a Level Sequence named LS_Bindings. Select an existing door or prop in the level and add it with Track (+), then Actor to Sequencer. This is a Possessable. Add keyframes to its Transform.
Drag a Skeletal Mesh or a Blueprint from the Content Browser into an empty area of Sequencer. Notice the lightning bolt icon. This is a Spawnable.
Right-click the possessable prop and choose Convert to Spawnable. Play the sequence and watch the Outliner as the actor appears and disappears.

Right-click the spawnable track, open the Spawnable category and set Spawned Object Owner to External. Play again and confirm that the actor stays after the sequence ends. Then set it back to This Sequence.
On the Spawn track, trim the section so that the actor spawns 1 second after the sequence starts.
Right-click a possessable track and open Assign Actor. Use Replace with Selected to bind the track to a different actor of the same class.
Extra: use Convert Selected Binding(s) To and choose Replaceable from Director Blueprint, then Quick Bind, then Resolve to Player Pawn. Test it in Play In Editor.
CQ21.done_when: Send a screenshot of Sequencer that shows one possessable track and one spawnable track (with the lightning bolt visible), the Spawnable properties panel open, and the Outliner during playback. Add three sentences: one case where you would use a possessable, one case where you would use a spawnable, and what changes when Spawned Object Owner is set to External.

CQ22.brief: Many cinematic shots use a camera that follows the subject. The Cine Camera Actor can turn by itself to keep an actor in view (Look at Tracking) and keep that actor sharp (Tracking focus). A rail or a crane can carry the camera along with the action. In this quest you set up a tracking camera, put it on a rail, add a crane shot, and add a little noise so that one camera feels handheld.
checklist: Create a Level Sequence named LS_Follow. It needs a moving character or a prop that travels across the set.

Add a Cine Camera Actor named CAM_Track. In Current Camera Settings, open Lookat Tracking Settings and enable Look at Tracking. Set Actor to Track to the character, and set a Relative Offset so that the head is framed. Enable Draw Debug Look at Tracking Position to check the point the camera aims at.
Set Look at Tracking Interp Speed to a value above 0. Compare how the camera follows with this value and with 0.
Set Focus Method to Tracking and choose the same actor. Enable Draw Debug Focus Plane and Smooth Focus Changes.

Place a Camera Rig Rail. Add spline points and curve the track. Attach CAM_Track by dragging it onto the rail in the Outliner. Add the rail to Sequencer and keyframe Current Position on Rail from 0 to 1.
Add a Camera Rig Crane with a second camera named CAM_Crane. Keyframe Crane Pitch, Crane Yaw and Crane Arm Length so that the camera rises and reveals the scene.
On the Transform track of one camera, right-click a rotation channel and choose Override with Double Perlin Noise. This adds small random movement for a light handheld feel. Set a low Amplitude.
CQ22.done_when: Send a screenshot of the viewport with the debug look-at cube and the rail visible, and a screenshot of Sequencer that shows the rail, crane and camera tracks with keys. Add a short note that says which Interp Speed you chose and why.

CQ23.brief: This quest is a complete scene that you take from an empty level to graded final frames. It uses everything from the earlier quests: shots, an animated character, following cameras, lighting for each shot, color grading, and a final render. You build a scene of 30 to 45 seconds and write a short breakdown that explains your choices.
checklist: Build a scene of 30 to 45 seconds named LS_Scene_Master. It needs at least 3 shots in a Shots track, and each shot is its own Level Sequence.
Put one animated character in the scene, with an Animation track that has at least 2 clips. Characters, cameras and shot lights must be Spawnables.
Use at least one following camera (Look at Tracking, a rail or a crane) and one static camera. Place your cuts on an action, not at random moments.
Light each shot with spawnable lights. Use a lighting channel for the hero in at least one shot. Lock the exposure with Manual metering.
Grade the picture. Use one base Post Process Volume for the look of the project, and at least one grade for a single shot with a different Priority.
Render with Movie Render Queue. Render a PNG sequence and EXR files, with a Temporal Sample Count of at least 4 and TAA disabled. Save the settings as a preset named MRQ_Scene.
Encode the PNG files to a video with any tool. Write a half-page breakdown with the shot list, what each camera does, what the grade does, and your render settings.
CQ23.done_when: Send a video link or file (30 to 45 seconds), a screenshot of the master sequence in Sequencer with the shots expanded, a screenshot of the MRQ settings, and your written breakdown. A mentor reviews it live.

CQ24.brief: A scene without sound feels unfinished. In Sequencer, an Audio Track holds sound clips on the same timeline as the picture, so music and effects stay in sync with the cuts. A sound can also be attached to an actor, so that it seems to come from that actor in the 3D world. In this quest you add music and a sound effect, fade and loop them, attach one to a character, and render the sound to a file.
checklist: Open a sequence that has a character and at least 2 shots. Add an Audio Track with Track (+) and drop a music Sound Wave at frame 0.
Add a second Audio Track for a footstep sound or a door sound. Trim its edges, and drag its end past the length of the clip so that it loops.
Drag the upper corners of the music section to make a fade in and a fade out. Then make two clips overlap and adjust the crossfade handles.

Expand the sound-effect track and set Attach to the character. Right-click the section, open Properties, and set an Attenuation Settings asset, which makes the sound quieter with distance. Move the camera away and listen to how the sound gets quieter.
Use Start Frame Offset (hold Shift and drag) to slide the sound inside its section, so that it lands exactly on the frame of the footstep.
Add the WAV Audio export to your MRQ job and render 5 seconds together with a PNG sequence.
CQ24.done_when: Send a screenshot of Sequencer with both audio tracks, with the fades and the crossfade visible and the Attach and Attenuation settings shown. Also send a screenshot of the output folder with the .wav file next to the PNG frames. Add one line that says what you did if the trimmed clip did not play correctly.
